questions.stem: A client with diabetes is prescribed a beta-blocker and says tachycardia is a main warning sign used to recognize hypoglycemia. What should the nurse teach?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Expect beta-blocker therapy to make tachycardia a more reliable warning of hypoglycemia, so pulse changes can be trusted more strongly.","B":"Teach that beta-blockers may mask some hypoglycemia warning signs, so glucose monitoring remains important when symptoms are less obvious.","C":"Teach that beta-blockers eliminate the need for glucose monitoring because clinically important hypoglycemia becomes unlikely during treatment.","D":"Expect beta-blockers to prevent hypoglycemia during exercise or missed meals, so routine glucose checks can safely be reduced."}}
questions.rationale: Current insulin labeling notes that antiadrenergic drugs such as beta-blockers can reduce or eliminate some signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia. Option B is correct because it warns that symptom recognition may be blunted and reinforces glucose monitoring. Option A incorrectly makes tachycardia more reliable. Option C incorrectly removes monitoring. Option D incorrectly states that beta-blockers prevent hypoglycemia.
questions.source_name: DailyMed / FDA Label — HUMULIN R (insulin human) injection
questions.source_detail: Current HUMULIN R prescribing information lists antiadrenergic drugs including beta-blockers and states that signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia may be reduced or absent; the label was updated May 27, 2025.

qc.qc_note: Strict final audit: max/min option-character ratio <=1.15; keyed option within 10% of distractor mean; keyed option is neither shortest nor longest; distractors manually reviewed for clinical plausibility, grammatical parallelism, and answer-cue leakage.
